For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

:::

Full text

Abstract

Paul E. Meehl's crud factor posits that variables in the social and behavioural sciences are never entirely unrelated, encapsulated in the notion that "everything correlates with everything". This preregistered systematic review examined how the crud factor and Lykken's related concept of ambient noise have been defined, interpreted, and applied across research fields.

We identified 424 works through database searches and citation tracking and analysed conceptual attributes and citation intentions. Among works allowing an inference about the relationship between the two concepts, the crud factor and ambient noise were almost uniformly treated as interchangeable, and both were most frequently invoked to argue that nullhypothesis significance testing against an exact-zero effect is unsuitable for corroborating theories. Reported numerical conventions for the crud factor varied widely, indicating no established empirical benchmark. Based on the synthesis, we propose an operational definition within the multitrait-multimethod validation framework: narrow-sense crud comprises heterotrait-heteromethod associations unexplained by substantive theory or theories of methodological artifacts, whereas broad-sense crud additionally encompasses heterotraitmonomethod associations and thus method-related covariance. This distinction provides a basis for empirically estimating the magnitude of the crud factor and evaluating its methodological implications.

1. Introduction

>Introduction

1.1. The crud factor: Three attempts at definition, still no clarity

Across the vast landscape of psychological research, an intriguing and persistent mystery threads through the fabric of the discipline-a phenomenon Paul Meehl (1984) famously termed the crud factor: a hidden web of interconnections, an omnipresent network of causal structures so intricate and elusive that it connects seemingly unrelated phenomena in incomprehensible ways. Meehl (1990b) introduced the crud factor in the context of a list of ten obfuscating factors that render most findings in psychology uninterpretable. Metaphorically speaking, the crud factor could also be likened to specks of dust on a scientist's microscope lens. As the scientist examines one subject after another, these particles remain constant, creating an ever-present distortion. In Goethe's Faust, the protagonist longs to achieve "That I may detect the inmost force / Which binds the world, and guides its course" (Goethe, 1808 (Goethe, /2018, p. , p. 2)-a poetic ambition that appears to parallel Meehl's recognition of the pervasive, unseen forces linking everything with everything.

The idea of the crud factor has some predecessors. Prior to Meehl, Lykken (1968) already had introduced a related concept which he termed ambient noise, describing it as the shared variance of unrelated variables. According to Lykken (1968), this ambient noise arises from an accumulation of factors such as correlations between psychological and physical variables, experimenter bias, and common method variance. This concept of ambient noise seems to have influenced Meehl's notion of the crud factor, as both he and Lykken-in their dedication to improve research methodology-corresponded on the notion that, in a sense, "everything is related to everything else". Lykken's concept of ambient noise might, metaphorically speaking, represent the unavoidable background sound that accompanies any audio recording, frequencies shared across all recordings of different musical instruments, serving as a common thread among otherwise unrelated sources.

Half a century later, Orben and Lakens (2020) recently have significantly rekindled the interest in the concepts of crud factor and ambient noise through a scoping review. This recent narrative literature review highlighted a number of problems with the idea that "everything is related to everything", while also exploring citations of the concepts and perceived attributes and consequences in the manner of a traditional (i.e., not systematic) review. These researchers emphasized the relevance of the crud factor and ambient noise in psychological research, particularly drawing attention to a pervasive misunderstanding of the respective definition and implications. Specifically, they noted that the crud factor and ambient noise are often arbitrarily invoked to dismiss statistically significant yet small effects as trivial. Additionally, Orben and Lakens (2020) underscored the lack of empirical research and conceptual debate surrounding the notions of the crud factor and ambient noise, thereby advocating for a more nuanced understanding of their existence, consequences, and impact on empirical research practices.

An overview of extant definitions of the crud factor and ambient noise, as commonly understood, is displayed in Table 1.

From this ensemble of definitions it is clear that so far no precise and commonly accepted operational definition of the crud factor and ambient noise seem to have been established. It is this gap (i.e., conceptual clarification) that the current paper seeks to address.

The evident ambiguity surrounding the attempts of definition (Table 1) may well arise from the core of the concept itself: both the crud factor and ambient noise are grounded in the foundational idea that everything is interconnected in ways too complex to fully comprehend or to theorize explicitly.

Consequently, the crud factor and ambient noise should be understood as residual categories whose scope depends on the theories available at a given time. They refer to empirical associations that are not currently accounted for by a specific theoretical explanation. Their content is therefore defined negatively-by what is not yet theoretically explained-rather than positively by a stable set of phenomena. As psychological theories develop, effects previously classified as the crud factor or ambient noise may be isolated, conceptually specified, and incorporated into a theoretical framework. Once this occurs, they no longer belong to these residual categories. Thus, the crud factor and ambient noise are practical labels for what remains theoretically unaccounted for at a particular stage of scientific development. Similar to how mathematics, though not a natural science, is indispensable for advancing physics, the crud factor and ambient noise might serve as a methodological aid to address the complexities inherent in the psychological and social sciences. Consequently, investigating the crud factor and ambient noise relies heavily on understanding how it is perceived and utilized within the scientific community.

As depicted in Figure 1, the two key papers of Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), as well as the much more recent review by Orben and Lakens (2020), continue to garner attention within the scientific community, thus underscoring the growing recognition of the crud factor and ambient noise concepts and their implications. Citation trends suggest that references to the crud factor have increased markedly since the early 2010s, a development that appears closely aligned with the onset of the replication crisis and the broader confidence debate in psychology. However, the specific research fields wherein these influential works are cited have yet to be analysed systematically. Exploring this citation landscape presents a valuable opportunity to determine whether the impact of these two concepts remains primarily within psychology or extends to other disciplines in similar vein. Such an analysis would provide critical insights into how the crud factor and ambient noise are understood and applied across various research fields, thereby offering a more comprehensive perspective on their interdisciplinary influence.

1.2. Methodological considerations regarding Orben and Lakens (2020)

First important steps towards such an elucidation of the meaning and impact of the crud factor and ambient noise have been made by Orben and Lakens (2020), who examined how the crud factor has been cited in the research literature, focusing on whether particular attributes were associated with its appearance, invocation, and use. Specifically, they coded whether a paper characterized the crud factor as representing "non-real" or "trivial" relationships, attributed it to methodological factors such as common method variance or experimental error, relied exclusively on Meehl's statement that "everything correlates with everything else" as a definition, or reported a numerical crud estimate. Except for the numerical value of the crud estimate, these variables were coded dichotomously as present ("Y") or absent ("N"). Importantly, an "N" in these researchers' coding scheme would only indicate that the respective characterization was not identified in the examined passage. However, this would not establish that the author explicitly endorsed the opposing position. For the "non-real" category, for example, an "N" may indicate either that the author regarded crud factor relationships as real or that the author did not comment on their reality. Similarly, an "N" for common method variance may indicate either that the author explicitly distinguished the crud factor from methodological artifacts or that the relationship between these concepts was not addressed. The binary coding scheme is therefore suitable for determining how frequently particular characterizations appeared in the literature, but it cannot distinguish an explicit rejection of a characterization from the absence of any relevant statement.

This distinction is important when interpreting the predominance of "N" codes in the dataset: "non-real" (Y: 24, N: 165), "common method variance" (Y: 19, N: 170), "quote only" (Y: 48, N: 141), and "crud estimate" (Y: 33, N: 156). These frequencies indicate that the respective attributes were not explicitly present in most examined passages; they do not demonstrate that most authors endorsed the corresponding opposite positions. For instance, Smith (2018) invoked the crud factor, but did not discuss whether common method variance forms part of it.

Coding this passage as "N" is consistent with Orben and Lakens' (2020) coding framework, because no association with common method variance was stated. However, this code cannot establish whether Smith (2018) explicitly excluded common method variance from the crud factor or simply did not address the issue.

The present review extends this approach by distinguishing among explicit endorsement, explicit rejection, and no comment. This three-category coding scheme preserves the information captured by Orben and Lakens (2020) while additionally separating substantive conceptual positions from cases in which no position can be inferred. It therefore allows for a more precise assessment of how authors conceptualize the reality of crud factor relationships and their relation to methodological sources of covariance.

Orben and Lakens (2020) emphasized that their review was not designed to quantify relationships among the coded variables, but rather as a scoping-review exercise intended to describe how the crud factor had been used in the literature. Their procedure was closely based on the PRISMA 2009 statement (Moher et al., 2009). Orben and Lakens (2020) further called for the development of methods that could distinguish crud-like associations from theoretically meaningful relationships. To this end, they outlined descriptive approaches, such as visualizing distributions of background correlations in histograms, and inferential approaches, such as using likelihood ratios to assess whether an observed correlation is more consistent with a hypothesized effect-size distribution or with a distribution of crud-like associations. Most importantly for the present discussion, however, although their article was entitled "Crud (re)defined," the authors provided a conceptual definition of the crud factor and a separate definition of the crud estimate, but not a validated operational procedure that would allow researchers to identify or isolate the crud factor unambiguously in empirical datasets.

1.3. Properties of the crud factor and its consequences

Several unresolved questions concern the conceptual scope of the crud factor and ambient noise, as well as their consequences for psychological inference. These questions include whether the two terms denote the same phenomenon, which types of associations and sources of covariance they encompass, and how their presumed existence affects the interpretation of statistical results.

In particular, the relationship between the terms crud factor and ambient noise might be a case of jangle fallacy, a phenomenon where a single construct is given different labels (Hanfstingl et al., 2024; Marsh, 1994). Orben and Lakens (2020) seem to exhibit ambiguity in their treatment of the crud factor and ambient noise. They partially conflate the two, treating them at times as a single concept, evident in their statement "To give credit for this idea to any single researcher" (Orben & Lakens, 2020, p. 239), and referred educated guesses about the magnitude of the crud factor not only to Meehl, but also to Lykken. Conversely, they also distinguish between the two, referring specifically to "Lykken's concept of ambient noise" (Orben & Lakens, 2020, p. 243) and "Meehl's original definition of the crud factor" (Orben & Lakens, 2020, p. 238). The distinction between the concepts was not made by Meehl himself, who wrote of "the ubiquitous crud factor, what David T. Lykken (1968) calls the 'ambient correlational noise' in social science" (Meehl, 1990b, p. 208), and earlier also wrote that what "Lykken calls the 'ambient noise,' or 'crud factor,' is of unknown average value" (Meehl, 1986, p. 327).

A further issue related to the crud factor is the appropriateness of null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST) against an exact-zero effect, in order to corroborate theoretical claims. Given the presumed absence of genuine exact-zero effects in complex psychological systems, testing against an exact-zero effect becomes, as Bakan (1966) argued, fundamentally flawed. The p value against the null hypothesis in the NHST framework represents the probability of obtaining empirical results (or more extreme ones) under the assumption that the stochastic mechanism in the background is parametrized with an exact-zero effect. Since NHST only accounts for sampling error, the presence of pervasive non-zero relationships would render statistical significance against an exact-zero effect entirely dependent on statistical power, reducing the test to a mere function of sample size.

Physical-background analogies have been used to illustrate this problem. For example, Smiley et al. (2023) compare the relevant background variation to photon noise or cosmic microwave background radiation. Such analogies portray the crud factor as a persistent background of small associations that accompanies empirical measurement. However, they do not establish that this background has a fixed lower bound or a universal magnitude. The metaphor should therefore be distinguished from Lykken's specific term ambient noise and should not be treated as an operational definition.

The functional form and magnitude of crud-like associations also remain unclear. The concept does not specify whether the relevant dependencies are exclusively linear, and a Pearson correlation captures only the bivariate linear component of an association. More complex multivariate causal structures may therefore not be adequately represented by a single correlation coefficient. A separate question is whether the magnitude of the crud factor varies across research domains and measurement instruments. Meehl (1990a, p. 124) explicitly suggested that "the average correlation of any randomly picked pair of variables in social science depends on the domain, and also on the instruments employed". Consequently, a single universal benchmark may be inappropriate, and the extent to which the literature treats the crud factor as domain-or instrument-dependent requires systematic examination.

A further conceptual issue is whether methodological artifacts form part of the crud factor. Orben and Lakens (2020) excluded common method variance and experimental error because they interpreted Meehl's crud factor as comprising only "real" correlations. This conclusion depends on how real is defined. If the term is reserved for substantive psychological relationships, method-induced associations are excluded. If real means replicable, however, systematic method effects may qualify, even though they do not reflect substantive psychological relations between constructs. Methodological artifacts might nevertheless be excluded on a different ground: unlike crud-like associations, they can be explained by established methodological mechanisms. Meehl's description of crud as "real (replicable) correlations" therefore does not fully resolve this boundary (Meehl, 1990a, p. 125). However, given its frequent use to dismiss significant, but small effects (Brown & Coyne, 2018; Diseth & Martinsen, 2009), it is worth questioning whether the scientific community perceives the crud factor and ambient noise as real constructs or as theoretical tools to critique methodological practices.

Common method variance refers to systematic variance attributable to a shared measurement method, which may inflate or deflate observed relationships between constructs (Podsakoff et al., 2003 (Podsakoff et al., , 2024)). Experimenter bias similarly denotes systematic effects of researchers' expectations or behaviour on data collection. Lykken (1968) included both sources in ambient noise, whereas Meehl treated experimenter bias separately from the crud factor. His discussion of "methods covariance" does not clearly establish whether he considered it part of crud. The inclusion of methodological artifacts therefore remains an open conceptual question.

The applicability of the concepts crud factor and ambient noise to correlational variables (i.e., variables examined in non-experimental designs) versus experimentally manipulated variables remains a further subject of debate. Meehl (1990b) argued that the crud factor primarily affects correlational studies, as they rely on non-experimental data where spurious correlations are omnipresent, thereby implying that experimental manipulation could eliminate the influence of the crud factor. Conversely, Lykken (1968) suggested that ambient noise extends to experimental designs, arising from factors such as various methodological artifacts. This raises the question of whether the scientific community perceives these omnipresent relationships as still present when variables are rigorously experimentally varied. Lykken (1968) further mentioned that ambient noise should be influenced by both psychological state variables (e.g., exhaustion) and trait variables (e.g., personality characteristics), but did not elaborate further on the details of this idea. It thus remains unclear whether scientists consistently perceive the crud factor and ambient noise as being dependent on both trait and state variables or not.

More generally, the above conceptual differences and uncertainties raise the overarching question of whether these concepts as such are indeed used in alignment with the definitions provided in the key papers on this theme (Lykken, 1968; Meehl, 1990b), or if they are applied more or less unsophisticatedly to dismiss significant findings. Beyond examining the conceptual properties of the crud factor and ambient noise and their alignment with foundational definitions, it is crucial to understand the motivations behind their citation, such as the rationale for inclusion or the purpose they serve within a publication. These intentions provide critical insights into how the concepts are perceived and utilized within the research community, thus reflecting their functional role in scientific discourse.

1.4. The present systematic review

This systematic review attempted to illuminate the (to some extent, blurred, opaque, if not outright enigmatic) concepts of the crud factor and ambient noise in a comprehensive way (unprecedented in scale, scope, and methodological approach), being the first to employ a robust methodological framework with the inclusion criteria for the pertinent literature and a qualitative analysis schema laid out a priori. The review addressed two central research questions: (1) What definition of the crud factor emerges from a synthesis of the literature, how has this conceptualization evolved over time, and how does it relate to ambient noise? (2) How have the crud factor and ambient noise been applied across publication periods and research fields? Given the conceptual focus of these questions, relevant passages were extracted verbatim to preserve authors' original wording and make definitional ambiguities transparent.

The study protocol was preregistered on June 14, 2024, during the pilot stage of the review (in which preliminary Google Scholar searches were used to develop and test the coding scheme, as stated in the preregistration), at the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/pw9sa), utilizing the Generalized Systematic Review Registration Form (van den Akker et al., 2023) as an appropriate template. This preregistration form specifies the review type (systematic mapping review), search strategy (databases, search strings, descendancy approach), inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction schema, research questions, coding categories (of properties and consequences), and planned synthesis methods.

The current systematic review expands on the scoping review by Orben and Lakens (2020) by incorporating additional categories of analysis (see Table 2). These include the interchangeable mention and use of the crud factor and ambient noise, the appropriateness of NHST against an exact-zero effect to corroborate theories, and the research-field dependency of the crud factor and ambient noise. Other aspects analysed are the inclusion of experimenter bias, psychological trait and state variables, presence in correlational or experimental variables, the perceived realness of the concepts, whether the concepts were cited correctly, and various semantic categories of citation intentions. In addition, this review links definitional attributes to whether the work focused on the crud factor, ambient noise, or both, and whether the work cited one or both of the key papers (Lykken, 1968; Meehl, 1990b).

Orben and Lakens (2020) coded whether selected characterizations were present or absent in the examined passages. This binary approach was suitable for estimating the prevalence of these characterizations, but it did not distinguish an explicit rejection from the absence of any relevant statement. Because the present review aims to compare endorsement and rejection of specific conceptual propositions, each proposition was coded as agreement, disagreement, or no comment. This three-category scheme provides a more fine-grained account of authors' stated positions without implying that the earlier binary coding misrepresented the source material. Because the terms crud factor and ambient noise are frequently used interchangeably, we expected broadly similar patterns of coded positions across works discussing either concept.

2. Method

>Method

2.1. Literature search strategies and inclusion criteria

These were predefined and included in the study preregistration (https://osf.io/pw9sa). Systematic searches were conducted between June 12 and June 24, 2024, in the following literature databases: Web of Science/Clarivate, Scopus, PubMed, EBSCOhost, ScienceDirect, Association for Computing Machinery (ACM), Medline, dimensions.ai, and Google Scholar, using the search strings "crud factor" OR "crud estimate" OR ("ambient noise" AND "Lykken"); records from all sources were merged and deduplicated on June 27, 2024. Additionally, using a citation-context analysis (following González-Teruel & Abad-García, 2018), works citing the key papers of Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968) were identified via Google Scholar and included as well. In a supplementary search (October 4, 2024), works citing the scoping review by Orben and Lakens (2020) were identified in the same way and included, provided they had not already been To increase specificity, only works that mentioned the terms "crud factor" or "ambient noise" at least once in the text (with the reference list omitted), were included in the analysis. Because this review maps how two concepts have been defined, interpreted, and applied rather than synthesizing empirical effects, no risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted (as preregistered).

To assess search coverage, the works in the scoping review by Orben and Lakens (2020) were used as a reference set, and each was matched against the present corpus. Works not retrieved in the present review were checked against the screening records to determine whether they had been retrieved, but excluded, or not retrieved at all. Data files were additionally checked for plausibility with the assistance of a large language model (see Declaration of AI use); all flagged records were re-examined manually by the first author.

Deviations from the preregistration.

Works citing Orben and Lakens (2020) that had not already been identified through the database search or through citation tracking of Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968) were subsequently included as a further source of records, which yielded 24 of the 424 included works.

The inclusion criterion was tightened from the occurrence of the words crud or ambient to the occurrence of the full terms crud factor or ambient noise outside the reference list, in order to increase specificity (e.g., some works' reference lists included Orben and Lakens, 2020, or Ferguson and Heene, 2021, without the citing work itself referring to the crud factor).

The search strings were corrected after the comparison with Orben and Lakens (2020) showed that the preregistered search string had not been processed as intended in Google Scholar: Google Scholar did not apply the nested Boolean operator ("ambient noise" AND "Lykken"), so that the term "Lykken" was effectively applied to all search terms and works mentioning the crud factor without mentioning Lykken were not retrieved. On October 5, 2026, the Google Scholar search was supplemented with corrected search strings ("crud factor" -Lykken; "crud estimate" -Lykken; see Deviations from the preregistration). Excluding "Lykken" only removed records that had already been retrieved by the original search, so that the original and the supplementary searches together implement the preregistered search logic. All records retrieved in this way were screened and coded using the same procedures and inclusion criteria; this supplementary search contributed 70 of the 424 included works.

The protocol foresaw exploratory inferential tests alongside the descriptive synthesis.

Because the coding categories were dominated by no-comment classifications, with several cells empty and expected frequencies below conventional thresholds throughout, such tests could not be validly computed, and analyses were restricted to descriptive statistics. The protocol specified that the review would synthesize existing definitions; the operational definition proposed in Section 4.3 goes beyond this synthesis and was developed post hoc, on the basis of the reviewed material but not derived from it by any preregistered procedure.

2.2. Data extraction

One researcher (R.B.) extracted the data for this review. A second coder (C.E.) independently coded a random sample of 30 works, yielding 35 paired concept-specific coding units because works addressing both the crud factor and ambient noise were coded separately.

Given the strongly imbalanced category distributions and the predominance of no-comment classifications, intercoder agreement was summarized using percentage agreement. Across the 15 coding variables, the median value of agreement was 88.6% (IQR = 84.3%-95.7%; range = 25.7%-100%); these values refer to the initial codings before consensus discussion. Agreement was at least 77.1% for 13 of the 15 variables, whereas lower for the perceived reality of the focal concept (54.3%) and its presence in correlational research (25.7%). The latter discrepancy reflected different initial decision rules: C.E. inferred inclusion from references to correlational measures, whereas R.B. required an explicit textual link between the focal concept and correlational research. Following discussion, the coders adopted the explicit-link criterion and recoded the affected cases accordingly. All remaining disagreements were resolved by consensus before the final analyses.

2.3. Identification of relevant text passages, decision rules, and argumentative relationships

If a key paper was cited multiple times within a work, only passages in which the citation concerned the crud factor or ambient noise were included. For example, if Meehl (1990b) was cited once in relation to the proposition that "everything correlates with everything" and elsewhere in relation to loose derivation chains without reference to the crud factor, only the former citation was included. Statements appearing outside the immediate citation passage were attributed to the crud factor or ambient noise only when the text explicitly linked them to the concept.

An argumentative relationship was generally inferred when the focal concept and the relevant statement occurred within the same paragraph. Statements across paragraphs were linked to the focal concept only when an explicit textual connection, such as a causal (e.g., "because of this bias," "this leads to..."), inferential (e.g., "this suggests that...," "consequently..."), or anaphoric (i.e., a pronoun or definite noun phrase, such as "this effect" or "it," referring back to an earlier mention of the crud factor or ambient noise) reference, established that the statement concerned the crud factor or ambient noise. Mere cooccurrence within the same work was insufficient. The link could occur within a paragraph or across adjacent paragraphs. Mere co-occurrence of a discussion of the crud factor and another issue, such as the appropriateness of NHST, was insufficient for coding an argumentative relationship. Works that mentioned the crud factor or ambient noise but cited a key paper for an unrelated purpose were excluded from analyses based on citations of the key papers but retained in analyses based on explicit mentions of the crud factor and ambient noise.

2.4. Research fields and types of included work

Research fields were operationalized using the Web of Science categories assigned by Clarivate to the source publication, where available. These categories reflect source-level indexing-for example, of journals or books-rather than a content-based classification of individual works. A source publication could be assigned to multiple Web of Science categories, all of which were retained. For example, a source could be classified under Education & Educational Research, Social Sciences, Mathematical Methods, and Psychology, Mathematical.

Cumulative frequencies were plotted to describe publication trends over time across these categories. Publication type was classified separately as journal article, book, thesis, or online publication (e.g., websites). 10) estimates or benchmarks provided for the magnitude of the crud factor. It should be noted that in many of the included works the crud factor or ambient noise was only mentioned briefly and not elaborated in more detail. Consequently, because of the relatively large number of categories coded per work, the majority of entries were expected to fall into the no comment category, not because categories were missing, but because the available information was too sparse.

To illustrate the coding procedure, consider the category "interchangeable usage of the crud factor and ambient noise": The crud factor and ambient noise are considered interchangeable (coded as1 = Yes) when their usage implies equivalence through verbal cues, e.g., "ambient noise, also called crud factor", or "Lykken (1968) called this ambient noise, while Meehl referred to it as the crud factor". Additionally, this field would have been coded as1 = Yes, if the crud factor was backed up with citing the ambient noise paper of Lykken (1968) or ambient noise with citing the crud factor paper of Meehl (1990b), thereby implying equivalence and interchangeable usage of these concepts. The field would have been coded as0 = No, if the two concepts were clearly distinguished from each other (e.g., "due to crud factor or ambient noise", where the "or" indicates distinct causes). In cases of doubt, the field was conservatively coded as0 = No. When both concepts were treated interchangeably, but only one was elaborated upon, the elaboration was attributed to both, resulting in two entries in the extraction file. If a work only referred to one of the concepts, without implying any connection to the other, the field was coded as no comment. The complete coding criteria for all categories are provided in Table 3.

2.6. Data synthesis and analysis

All analyses were descriptive; no inferential statistics were computed. Coded attributes are reported as absolute frequencies and percentages of the relevant denominator. Because most works commented on only a subset of the coded categories, percentages for the perceived attributes refer to the 483 concept-specific coding entries, whereas percentages describing the corpus as a whole refer to the 424 included works; the relevant denominator is stated with each result.

For works that mentioned the crud factor or ambient noise or cited Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968), cumulative plots were used to visualize publication trends over time (see Section 3.2.3). The steepness of a curve represents the rate at which publications were added annually, whereas its absolute height represents the total number of contributions up to a given year. For the analyses by research field, source publications assigned to several Web of Science categories contribute to each of them, so the field-specific counts sum to more than the number of works. Because the most recent searches were conducted in August and October 2026, the final year is incomplete and the curves are truncated accordingly.

Analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2024) using the packages readxl (Wickham & Bryan, 2023) and openxlsx (Schauberger & Walker, 2024) for data import, dplyr (Wickham et al., 2023), tidyr (Wickham et al., 2024), and stringr (Wickham, 2023) for data preparation, ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016), patchwork (Pedersen, 2024), ggVennDiagram (Gao et al., 2024) and grid (R Core Team, 2024) for the figures, and knitr (Xie, 2024) and kableExtra (Zhu, 2024) for tabular output.

The analysis scripts and the extraction file are available at https://osf.io/qxet5/files/osfstorage. Data preparation and construction of the analytical subsets were additionally performed using KNIME Analytics Platform (Berthold et al., 2009); the corresponding workflow is available in the OSF repository.

2.7. Citation intentions

The reasons for citing Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968) in connection with the crud factor or ambient noise were examined using citation-context analysis, following González-Teruel and Abad-García (2018). The preregistration specified an initial set of citation-intention categories, included an open category for other citation reasons, and explicitly allowed the classification scheme to be refined iteratively as additional motives emerged during the review. This refinement therefore formed part of the preregistered procedure rather than constituting a deviation.

The final classification distinguished whether citations intended: (1) to argue that a nonzero correlation remained compatible with discriminant validity because it fell within the expected range of the crud factor or ambient noise; (2) to argue that a correlation supported convergent validity because it exceeded that expected range; (3) to dismiss small effects as trivial; (4) to defend small effects as non-trivial; (5) to argue that theoretically predicted small effects remained meaningful; (6) to identify the crud factor or ambient noise as a problem for statistical modelling; (7) to claim that its estimated magnitude or detectability depended on sample size; and (8) to invoke the general notion that "everything is related to everything"; (9) to argue that NHST against an exact-zero effect is unsuitable for corroborating theories; and (10) to use the crud factor or ambient noise as a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI). Categories (8) to ( 10) emerged during the review process through the preregistered iterative-refinement procedure.

2.8. Assessment of correctness of citations of the key papers

Citations were evaluated against the definitions provided in the respective cited key papers, Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), and against Orben and Lakens's (2020) definition: "The epistemological concept that, in correlational research, all variables are connected through causal structures, which result in real nonzero correlations between all variables in any given data set" (p. 241).

Each assessment was coded dichotomously. A code of 1 indicated that the citation did not contradict any explicit definitional feature of the relevant reference standard, whereas a code of 0 indicated that at least one such feature was contradicted. Under the key-paper criterion, a citation to Lykken (1968) was coded as incorrect when it was used to exclude experimental research, because Lykken's conception of ambient noise encompassed both correlational and experimental research. The inclusion of common method variance was coded separately and was not treated as a citation error under this criterion because it is explicitly included in Lykken's ambient noise but remains ambiguous in relation to Meehl's crud factor.

3. Results

>Results

3.1. Study selection

The initial search (June 12-24, 2024) retrieved 717 records from the nine literature databases (dimensions.ai, n = 408; Google Scholar, n = 200; Scopus, n = 46; ScienceDirect, n = 34; EBSCOhost, n = 10; Web of Science, PubMed, and Medline, n = 6 each; ACM, n = 1). Citation tracking of the two key papers added a further 264 records (Meehl, 1990b, n = 189; Lykken, 1968, n = 75), yielding 981 records. A supplementary search on October 4, 2024 retrieved 68 records citing Orben and Lakens (2020), for a total of 1,049 records. An updated search conducted on August 11, 2026, repeating the same strategy for records published or indexed since the original search, retrieved a further 614 records: 240 from the nine databases (dimensions.ai, n = 122; Web of Science, n = 52; Scopus, n = 43; Google Scholar, n = 14; ScienceDirect, n = 4; PubMed, n = 2; EBSCOhost, ACM, and Medline, n = 1 each) and 374 from citation tracking (Meehl, 1990b, n = 209; Lykken, 1968, n = 125; Orben and Lakens, 2020, n = 40), for a combined total of 1,663 records. On October 5, 2026, the supplementary search with corrected search strings retrieved a further 412 records from Google Scholar ("crud factor" -Lykken, n = 402; "crud estimate" -Lykken, n = 10), resulting in 2,075 records in total.

Deduplication, performed by automated matching in EndNote 21 and subsequent manual inspection, removed 1,001 records (436 from the original search, 187 from the updated search, 286 from the search with corrected search strings, and 92 further duplicate entries identified during screening and data extraction), leaving 1,074 unique records for screening.

Records were excluded because ambient noise was used in its acoustic sense, denoting environmental sound rather than Lykken's concept (n = 97); because neither term appeared outside the reference list (n = 520); because crud was used in an unrelated sense (n = 30); because the full text could not be obtained (n = 2); or because the record was a preregistration without an accompanying work (n = 1), for a total of 650 exclusions. A total of 424 works met all inclusion criteria. Because works addressing both the crud factor and ambient noise were analysed separately for each concept, these 424 works yielded 483 concept-specific coding entries. Figure 2 presents the corresponding PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Page et al., 2021).

Search coverage was assessed against the 189 works included by Orben and Lakens (2020). The initial search of June 2024 retrieved 155 of these (relative recall 82.0%); the corrected search strings retrieved a further 23, so that 178 of 189 works (94.2%) were retrieved, all of which met the present inclusion criteria. The comparison also revealed errors in our own workflow, which were corrected: five retrieved works, among them McGrath (2005), had initially been excluded or marked as duplicates during screening. Of the 11 works not retrieved, one (Harms & Lakens, 2018) mentions neither the crud factor nor ambient noise; excluding it, relative recall was 178 of 188 (94.7%). Three of the remaining ten cite Meehl (1990b) but use only variants of the term ("crud", "crud level", "crud effect"), which were covered neither by the search strings nor by the inclusion criterion requiring the full term. The other seven use the exact term but were not retrieved because they are publication types whose full texts or reference lists are not (or not consistently) indexed by the databases searched: two doctoral dissertations, a government report, a preprint, a book, a workshop proceedings paper and a professional bulletin contribution. Among the works within the scope of the search strategy, the search thus retrieved 178 of 185 (96.2%). Relative recall should therefore be read as an estimate of the coverage of the present search strategy rather than as a reproduction of the earlier search.

3.2. Descriptive statistics 3.2.1. Number of references to the crud factor, ambient noise, and key papers in the included works

The subsequent analyses distinguish between works addressing the crud factor, ambient noise, or both, and between works citing Meehl (1990b), Lykken (1968), or both. Of the 424 unique works, 417 addressed the crud factor, 66 addressed ambient noise, and 59 addressed both. Because works addressing both concepts contributed one entry for each concept, analyses of concept-specific attributes comprised 483 entries: 417 concerning the crud factor and 66 concerning ambient noise. Among the 236 works that cited at least one key paper, 215 (91%) cited Meehl (1990b), 57 (24%) cited Lykken (1968), and 36 (15%) cited both.

These frequencies are illustrated in Figure 3.

3.2.2. Overlap between concept mentions and citations of key papers

Figure 3 shows a close correspondence between mentions of the crud factor and citations of Meehl (1990b), as well as between mentions of ambient noise and citations of Lykken (1968). The difference between the number of works mentioning the crud factor and those citing Meehl (1990b) reflects works that referred to the concept using other sources. The smaller difference for ambient noise indicates that works mentioning this concept usually cited Lykken (1968). Overall, the crud factor was mentioned substantially more often than ambient noise.

3.2.3. Research field distribution of included works

The available Web of Science categories indicate that the included works were published in sources representing a broad range of research fields, including behavioural sciences, medicine, sociology, economics, and computer science (Figure 4). The cumulative trends suggest that references to the crud factor and ambient noise have increasingly extended beyond psychology. Of the 424 included works, 288 (68%) were journal articles or other papers, 69 (16%) were books or book chapters, 63 (15%) were dissertations or theses, and four (1%) were online publications.

3.2.4. Perceived attributes of the crud factor and ambient noise

This section compares perceived attributes across five analytical sets: (1) all conceptspecific entries concerning the crud factor or ambient noise, with entries addressing both concepts contributing one entry for each; (2) all entries concerning the crud factor; (3) all entries concerning ambient noise; (4) entries that cited Meehl (1990b); and (5) entries that cited Lykken (1968). The distribution of coded attributes was broadly similar across all five analytical sets (Figure 5). The most frequent coding outcome was no comment: for most works, the relevant passages did not provide sufficient information to infer agreement or disagreement regarding most predefined attributes. This reflects the typically brief treatment of the crud factor or ambient noise in these passages, rather than an absence of other substantive content in the works.

3.2.5. Interchangeable usage of crud factor and ambient noise

Among the 81 works that allowed an inference about the relationship between the two concepts, 77 (95%) treated the crud factor and ambient noise as interchangeable, whereas four (5%) treated them as distinct. Relative to the full corpus of 424 works, these corresponded to 18% and 1%, respectively.

3.2.6. Appropriateness of NHST against exact-zero effects to corroborate theories

Among the 483 concept-specific entries, 263 (54%) characterized NHST against an exact-zero effect as unsuitable for corroborating theories, none characterized it as suitable, and 220 (46%) provided no comment.

3.2.7. Inclusion of common method variance

Among the 483 concept-specific entries, 437 (90%) provided no comment on common method variance, 37 (8%) included it, and nine (2%) excluded it.

3.2.8. Inclusion of experimenter bias

For experimenter bias, 475 entries (98%) provided no comment, seven (1%) included it, and one (<1%) excluded it.

3.2.9. Inclusion of psychological trait and state variables

There was insufficient evidence of either the inclusion or exclusion of psychological trait and state variables in the concept of the crud factor. Among the 483 concept-specific entries, 473 (98%) provided no comment on the inclusion of psychological trait and state variables, nine (2%) included them, and one (<1%) excluded them.

3.2.10. Presence among correlational variables and experiments

Of the entries, 415 (86%) did not indicate whether correlational variables were considered part of the crud factor or ambient noise, and 449 (93%) did not clarify this for experimental designs. When such inferences were possible, correlational variables were more often included (67, 14%) than excluded (1, <1%). Experimental variables were also somewhat more often included (19, 4%) than excluded (15, 3%) (see Figure 5).

3.2.11. Research-field dependency

Among the 483 concept-specific entries, 22 (5%) indicated that the magnitude or nature of the focal concept depended on the research field, none indicated field independence, and 461 (95%) provided no comment.

3.2.12. Perception as a real phenomenon

When the reality of the crud factor or ambient noise was addressed, it was described as a real phenomenon in 66 of the 483 entries (14%) and as not real in 40 entries (8%).

3.2.13. Magnitude of the crud factor

The 61 works citing the crud factor in a way that allowed an inference about its perceived magnitude (e.g., dismissing a small but significant result as mere crud factor) referred to one of five papers to back up their claim (see Figure 6). Since these five papers were used as references, they can be considered fundamental sources of estimates of the magnitude of the crud factor, even though they may themselves provide only a very limited empirical basis (see Table 4). Lykken (1968) suggested that ambient noise might correspond to correlations of approximately r = .20, an estimate that was not empirically derived. Meehl (1990a) subsequently used r = .30 as an illustrative representative value of the crud factor for a worked power example, describing it as not an implausible value given the empirical examples he had just surveyed (MMPI intercorrelations in the middle-to-high .30s, among others [signed rather than absolute values, though nearly all were positive]). Meehl (1990b) repeated this same worked example, now explicitly grounding it in non-theory-driven correlations among MMPI scales of approximately r = .35 to .40 (again signed) and correlations of approximately r = .40 between MMPI scales and the Strong Vocational Interest Blank (explicitly an absolute-value mean), and extended the illustration to a second scenario (r = .40). Standing et al. (1991), analysing 135 variables in a sample of 2,058 students, found an average correlation of r = .07 (an explicit absolute-value grand mean; the underlying signed distribution was itself roughly symmetric around zero). More recently, Ferguson and Heene (2021) proposed a conservative lower-bound estimate of r = .10. In a large sample (N = 20,403), fifteen theoretically unrelated variables were correlated with a delinquency measure, and coefficients were aggregated as a mean absolute value via fixed-effects meta-analysis (r around .03 to .05). In a smaller sample (N = 4,899), the crud variables were unordered categorical variables with no meaningful direction, so correlations were instead expressed as R and, after partialling out age and gender as √𝜔 partial 2 , yielding r of around .11. These markedly different values illustrate the absence of a consistent empirical benchmark for the magnitude of the crud factor. This variability is unlikely to be a sampling artifact. Mean absolute correlations are inflated by sampling error, because taking absolute values folds chance negative correlations onto the positive side, so that sampling error can only raise, not lower, the mean. Meehl's (1990a Meehl's ( , 1990b) ) high values, however, do not hinge on such folding: his signed MMPI intercorrelations (r ≈ .35 to .40) were about as high as the absolutevalue mean between MMPI and Strong Vocational Interest Blank scales (r ≈ .40). Standing et al. (1991), in contrast, aggregated absolute values, so their estimate is subject to exactly this folding, and yet it is the smallest; correcting for it would make it even smaller and the discrepancy larger. At the same time, the higher values rest on a weak empirical basis: Lykken (1968) offered his estimate without data, and Meehl did not report the sample sizes underlying his figures. The differences therefore mainly reflect what was sampled (constructs sharing method or content variance, as in the MMPI, versus deliberately unrelated variables) and how rigorously the values were derived.

In the literature corpus for this review, the range of Pearson correlations used as a "convention" for crud factor estimates spanned from .07 (Onwuegbuzie & Daniel, 2002) to .60 (Capic et al., 2018), while the range for ambient noise estimates spanned from .10 (e.g., Miranda et al., 2025) to .50 (Cummins et al., 2018).

3.3. Citation context analysis

>Citation context analysis

3.3.1. Analysis of citation intentions per citation-context analysis

Both the key papers, Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), were cited to refer to the crud factor for mainly three reasons (see Table 5): (1) to argue that NHST against exact-zero effect is not suitable for corroborating theories (e.g., Ramsey & Ward, 2020); (2) to dismiss small, but significant effects (e.g., Burke, 1999); and (3), to claim that "everything is related to everything" (Pieters, 2017). In addition, Meehl (1990b) was also cited for various other purposes, such as to argue that the crud factor violates assumptions underlying statistical techniques (Ciarli et al., 2019), poses challenges in assessing construct validity (Hoyle et al., 2023), or is less relevant because common method variance (partly equated to the crud factor) is outweighed by measurement error (Lance et al., 2010). Similarly, Lykken (1968) was cited for various other reasons: for example, in Smiley and Kaiser (2024) to justify setting a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), a concept explained by Anvari and Lakens (2021); in Hermida (2015) to illustrate arbitrary choices of focal variables; and in Reith and Nehring (2020) as interchangeable with common method variance.

3.3.2. Correctness of citations of the key papers

Citations of Meehl (1990b) were evaluated against two reference standards (see Section 2.8 and Table 1): Meehl's own description and Orben and Lakens's (2020) definition, which restricts the crud factor to real nonzero correlations arising from causal structures in correlational research. Of 215 citations, 189 (88%) were correct and 26 (12%) incorrect according to Meehl (1990b), and 188 (87%) and 27 (13%), respectively, according to Orben and Lakens (2020).

The frequencies of correct citations are shown in Figure 7, and the respective definitions are provided in Table 1. Among the reasons for false citations, one error was the assertion that the crud factor was not real, but rather due to spurious correlations (Alexander, 2018). Another misinterpretation was the reduction of the crud factor to merely being a problem of multiple testing, as claimed by Burke (1999). Lykken (1968), which was cited in 57 included works, was correctly cited 53 times (93%) and incorrectly cited four times (7%) according to the paper's definition, and likewise 53 times (93%) correctly and four times (7%) incorrectly according to the interpretation provided by Orben and Lakens (2020). An example of a false citation of Lykken (1968), based on Lykken's own definition, is the exclusion of experimental variables, as highlighted in McMillan et al. (2008).

4. Discussion

>Discussion

4.1. The concepts of crud factor and ambient noise as a jangle fallacy

This systematic review examined how the crud factor has been defined, how its conceptualization has evolved over time, and how it has been applied across research fields.

Based on this synthesis, we propose a new operational definition. The sample of 424 works included here is more than twice as large as the 189 works included in Orben and Lakens (2020).

The various analyses mainly indicate that the crud factor and ambient noise are mostly used interchangeably, and thus appear to represent a historically based jangle fallacy; for this reason, they should not be considered two distinct constructs. This interpretation is supported by the broadly similar patterns of attributed properties across works referring to the crud factor, works referring to ambient noise, and the corresponding subsets citing Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968). Across these analytical sets, both concepts were most frequently associated with the view that NHST against an exact-zero effect is unsuitable for corroborating theories. Also, both concepts have been used for indicating that the phenomenon is relevant for variables from correlational research, but inconclusive for variables stemming from experimental studies.

Beyond this, if the inclusion of common method variance was touched on, it was included in both the crud factor and ambient noise. If a statement about the research-field dependency of the kind or magnitude of the crud factor or ambient noise was made, their research-field dependency was implied for both the crud factor and ambient noise. Also, both the crud factor and ambient noise were perceived as real in the sense of replicable phenomena. The reported range of conventions used to define the crud factor and ambient noise, sometimes invoked to dismiss statistically significant results, varied widely and appeared comparable across both concepts. The magnitudes that citing works attributed to the crud factor varied substantially.

These are not empirical estimates: the works did not investigate the crud factor themselves, but cited it in a way that revealed how large they took it to be (e.g., by treating effects up to a certain size as mere crud). The implied values ranged from below Cohen's (1988) threshold for a small effect (r = .07; Onwuegbuzie & Daniel, 2002) to above his threshold for a large effect (r = .60; Capic et al., 2018). The magnitudes implied for ambient noise ranged similarly, from r = .10 (e.g., Miranda et al., 2025) to r = .50 (Cummins et al., 2018).

4.2. The crud factor: Important, but rarely the focus

It is interesting to note that the crud factor apparently is not of central relevance for either the key papers of Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968) themselves, nor for the scientific community that cited these works. This conclusion is based on three main points: (1) neither of the key papers by Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), nor any other publications by these authors, were solely dedicated to the crud factor or ambient noise; ( 2) Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968) predominantly have been cited for reasons unrelated to the crud factor or ambient noise (even within the present search, which targeted these concepts, 520 screened records mentioned neither concept outside their reference list; see Section 3.1); and (3) neither Meehl (1990b) nor Lykken (1968) have provided precise definitions of the crud factor (or ambient noise) in their publications.

Although Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968) have been cited 1,183 and 1,806 times, respectively, according to Google Scholar (as of August 7, 2026), only 215 and 57 of these citing works, respectively, were included in the present systematic review (236 works in total) based on the predefined inclusion criteria. This discrepancy stems from the exclusion of citations that referenced these papers for reasons unrelated to the crud factor (or ambient noise), as the present review exclusively focused on works explicitly mentioning at least one of the concepts.

Both key papers addressed a wide range of topics beyond the crud factor (or ambient noise), with the majority of the respective citations referencing other aspects of their work. For instance, Lykken (1968) is often cited for its emphasis on the importance of replication in scientific research, whereas Meehl (1990b) is frequently referred to for his contribution to discussions about construct validity, nomological networks, as well as for the necessity of replication studies.

4.3. Operationally defining the crud factor

Inspection of the "conventions" offered for the crud factor revealed a preference towards clean first decimal numbers (e.g., r = .10, .20, .30), rather than empirically grounded benchmarks. Such conventions have even been invoked in order to dismiss sizeable effect sizes-that Cohen (1988) would have considered as moderate or large-as being merely (or likely) due to the crud factor.

In contrast, Funder and Ozer (2019) recently have argued quite to the contrary, in specifically suggesting that effects of r = .05, well below Cohen's small effect size benchmark, can still be practically meaningful if they accumulate over time or across individuals. Funder and Ozer (2019) proposed as an illustrative example that a slightly higher probability of positive social interactions for a person high in agreeableness can have cumulative relevance throughout their lifetime. Similarly, a minor improvement in a politician's presentation style during a television appearance reaching millions of viewers may well render tiny effects practically relevant. This tension among effect-size benchmarks suggests that Cohen's (1988) historical benchmarks indeed may require updating. While Funder and Ozer (2019) pushed towards recognizing the practical significance of quite small effects, conventions surrounding the crud factor often are used to dismiss even effects of moderate or large size.

In the same context, Anvari et al. (2023) debated conditions under which small observed effect sizes would generalize into practically relevant effects. On the one hand, amplifying mechanisms such as accumulation through repetition, cascading downstream consequences, or interactions with contextual factors can enlarge observed effects. On the other hand, counteracting mechanisms such as habituation, homeostatic regulation around set points, or compensatory responses can diminish them. Anvari et al. (2023) argued that researchers should make the underlying mechanisms they assume explicit and provide empirical justification for why amplifying or counteracting processes should dominate in a given case. Berggren and Flake (2026) recently showed that even in the absence of counteracting mechanisms, accumulation over time rests on highly restrictive assumptions (i.e., that the effect is causal, that no other stable causes influence the outcome, and that the effect does not vary within persons), which are unlikely to hold for psychological effects; long-term effects may even be smaller than those observed at a single time point.

Just as the lowered benchmark of what constitutes a relevant effect proposed by Funder and Ozer (2019) might apply to cases in which effect size accumulation can be expected, the crud factor may justify raising this threshold in cases where such accumulation is absent.

Hence, to address the lack of empirical evidence concerning the crud factor, here we propose a novel operational definition of the construct. This definition is based on the multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) framework, the classic approach for assessing construct validity through covariance analysis (Campbell & Fiske, 1959; for recent developments, see Helm, 2022; Marsh et al., 2026). The MTMM matrix includes correlations among several traits measured with several methods (at least two each are necessary), which, in turn, can be decomposed into trait variance and method variance. In the MTMM framework, heterotrait refers to different traits. For the present operationalization of the crud factor, we focus specifically on heterotrait associations for which no substantive relationship is theoretically expected. By contrast, monotrait refers to repeated measurements of the same trait. Likewise, the term heteromethod involves different measurement approaches (e.g., questionnaires, cognitive tests, behavioural observations), whereas the term monomethod relies on a single (i.e., the same) method. This distinction directly addresses a limitation noted by Orben and Lakens (2020), namely that distributions of background correlations alone do not separate crud-like associations from common method variance.

Building on this logic, we propose the following novel, twofold operational definition of the crud factor (Table 6). In its narrow sense, the crud factor, which excludes methodological artifacts, refers to correlations between different traits measured by different methods (i.e., heterotrait-heteromethod correlations) that cannot be explained by substantive theory or by theories of methodological artifacts. In its broad sense, the crud factor also includes correlations between different traits measured with the same method (i.e., heterotraitmonomethod correlations), thereby encompassing both narrow-sense crud correlations and correlations attributable to methodological artifacts. Importantly, both substantive theories and theories of methodological artifacts describe real, potentially replicable effects; the distinction concerns the source of the covariance rather than its reality. Because monomethod relationships may be affected by methodological artifacts, such as common method variance or experimenter bias, the broad-sense crud factor is represented by heterotrait-monomethod relationships (Table 6, quadrant C).

For example, consider the correlation between two theoretically unrelated personality traits, such as neuroticism and extraversion, when both are measured using the same method, usually self-report scales. In this case, any observed correlation would not only reflect the narrow-sense crud factor but also additional covariance attributable to the shared measurement method, thereby representing the crud factor in its broader sense. In contrast, the narrow-sense crud factor is the essence of heterotrait-heteromethod relationships (Table 6, quadrant D). For instance, it could be observed in the average nonzero correlation between neuroticism measured through self-reports and extraversion measured through informant reports.

The empirical disentanglement of the crud factor into its broad and narrow senses faces an additional challenge inherent in the MTMM framework. Campbell and Fiske (1959) anticipated covariance among methods (i.e., the non-orthogonality of different methods), implying that methods cannot be strictly classified as the same or different, but instead may share variance to varying degrees. For instance, both self-report and informant-report measures might overlap in that they are item-based and use Likert-type response formats. Similarly, different traits may also share genuine variance not attributable to methodological artifacts.

Consequently, the disentanglement of the crud factor into its broad and narrow components may constitute a mathematically underidentified problem, in which too many parameters (e.g., correlations among traits and methods, narrow-and broad-sense crud factor, and the reliability of measures) must be estimated simultaneously. Nonetheless, datasets including a sufficiently large number of distinct traits measured across different methods may provide lower-and upper-bound proxies for the magnitude of the crud factor, even if its broad and narrow components cannot be fully disentangled.

Having conceptually disentangled the crud factor with regard to methodological biases into its narrow and broad senses, the question remains how exactly crud factors should be quantified. It seems inappropriate that a phenomenon characterized by mysterious, omnipresent relationships too complex to be theorized could be adequately captured by statistical measures merely based on linearity assumptions, such as the classic Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, or on monotonicity assumptions, as via Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficient.

To move towards a solution, we recommend addressing this uncertainty through methodological multiplicity, that is, by quantifying the same associations with several coefficients that differ in the forms of association they detect. The Pearson product-moment correlation multiplies, for each person, the deviations from the means of both variables, sums these products, and standardizes the sum by the variability of both variables. It thus captures whether above-average values on one variable go along with above-average (or below-average) values on the other. Its range from -1 to +1 conveys the direction of an association and how closely the observations follow a straight line, and because deviations enter as products, it is sensitive to extreme observations. The Spearman rank-order correlation applies the same computation to ranks rather than to raw values; by retaining only the order of the values, it is suitable for nonlinear but monotonic relationships and less sensitive to extreme observations. Like Pearson's r, however, it cannot detect nonmonotonic relationships, such as U-shaped ones.

The distance correlation coefficient (dCor; Székely et al., 2007) closes this gap.
