Like the other two coefficients, it divides a covariance term by the variability of both variables, but uses their distance-based counterparts: the distance covariance (dCov) and the distance variances (dVar). Rather than comparing each person with the mean, however, it compares persons with each other, asking whether pairs of persons who are far apart on one variable also tend to be far apart on the other, regardless of the direction of these differences. Because the distance covariance, unlike the ordinary covariance, cannot become negative, distance correlation ranges from 0 to 1. Drawing on the distances among all pairs of persons rather than on deviations from the mean or on ranks, it is sensitive to forms of dependence that Pearson and Spearman correlations miss, and in the population, it equals zero if and only if the two variables are statistically independent.

In a pronounced inverted-U relationship, such as the one reported between extraversion and sales performance (Grant, 2013), persons with very low and very high extraversion may perform equally poorly, so that their contributions to Pearson's r cancel out; yet persons who are similar in extraversion remain similar in performance, and distance correlation detects this dependence. As illustrated in Figure 8, U-shaped, wave-shaped, and circular relationships, which leave Pearson and Spearman correlations near zero, are clearly identified by distance correlation. Moreover, distance correlation can quantify the dependence between entire sets of variables of different sizes, which neither Pearson nor Spearman correlations allow. Distance correlation does not, however, render the classical coefficients obsolete.

Because it ranges from 0 to 1, it conveys the strength but not the direction of a dependence, and its values are not directly comparable with those of Pearson correlations: for bivariate normal variables, distance correlation is a function of the absolute Pearson correlation and somewhat smaller than it (Székely et al., 2007), whereas in general, for any fixed Pearson correlation strictly between -1 and 1, distance correlation can take any value between 0 and 1 (Edelmann et al., 2021). Although introduced almost two decades ago, distance correlation is increasingly used and has only recently entered mainstream statistical software; for instance, it was first implemented in IBM SPSS Statistics in June 2025, with Version 31 (IBM Corp., n.d., 2025). For the crud factor, this versatility is particularly valuable. Meehl's notion of ubiquitous, theoretically unexplained relationships makes no assumption about their form, and there is no reason to expect such relationships to be exclusively linear or monotonic. Comparing distance correlation with Pearson and Spearman correlations therefore allows researchers to examine whether measures restricted to linear or monotonic associations capture the crud factor adequately or systematically underestimate it.

4.4. Implications

This systematic review underscores the relevance of the crud factor within and beyond psychology, revealing a persistent lack of definitional clarity, substantial variation in its assumed magnitude, and its often arbitrary use in interpreting empirical results. To address this gap, a new operational definition of the crud factor in its broad and narrow senses is proposed.

This constitutes a prerequisite for empirically estimating its magnitude, stability, and potential variability across research fields. Such estimates could serve as a SESOI, replacing the null value in NHST and providing meaningful thresholds for equivalence, non-inferiority, and nonsuperiority testing. Moreover, the crud factor may function as a minimum benchmark for assessing and establishing convergent and incremental validity, and as an upper boundary for divergent (discriminant) validity.

For instance, the broad-sense crud factor may be particularly informative as a reference point for evaluating higher-order personality models, such as the "Big One", or general factor, of personality. Musek (2007) proposed that the Big Five personality traits cannot only be reduced to the two higher-order dimensions of personality (namely, plasticity and stability), but even further to a single overarching factor representing the general integration of non-cognitive personality dimensions. In many studies following the pioneering paper of Musek (2007), personality constructs commonly are assessed using self-report questionnaires, meaning that analyses are exclusively based on monomethod data. This reliance on a single method underscores the potential relevance of the broad-sense crud factor as a baseline for interpreting any such findings derived from monomethod approaches.

On the level of metascientific investigations, research-field-specific estimates of the crud factor would enable further critical evaluations of effect-size conventions, such as the ones proposed by Cohen (1988) and, more recently, by Funder and Ozer (2019). In light of the replication crisis in science and the need for a metric to operationalize replication success (vs. failure), the crud factor could also serve as a benchmark for distinguishing successful from nonsuccessful replications. Once preliminary estimates of the crud factor become available, its broader metascientific implications could be explored through data-simulation approaches.

Such simulations could, for instance, explore publication dynamics through the lens of the crud factor, e.g., whether observed effects possibly represent false positives, as well as the underreporting of small, but meaningful effects due to inflated thresholds for what constitutes a small effect. The applications outlined in this section are proposals for future research rather than results of the present review; each presupposes that the crud factor can be estimated reliably and requires empirical validation for the specific inferential purpose.

4.5. Strengths and limitations

Study strengths include that this systematic review represents the first preregistered effort to clarify the concept of the crud factor, thus extending the predecessor scoping review by Orben and Lakens (2020) and setting a new benchmark for transparency, methodological rigour, and reproducibility in this domain. The significance of the topic, together with the substantial body of work addressing numerous aspects surrounding the crud factor, underscores the timeliness and necessity of this clarification attempt. By systematically analysing a corpus of 424 works, as compared to the 189 included in Orben and Lakens (2020), this review provides the most comprehensive examination of the crud factor to date, offering valuable insights into its conceptual properties and empirical implications while identifying patterns and gaps in the existing literature. Furthermore, by applying a three-way agreement/disagreement/no-comment coding scheme-agreement with a predefined proposition, disagreement with that proposition, or no comment-rather than the binary presence/absence coding used by Orben and Lakens (2020), this review provided a more fine-grained account of authors' stated positions.

As for study limitations, this review inter alia addressed an inherent challenge in studying the crud factor: the attempt at conceptual clarification is mainly based on how this phenomenon has been cited and interpreted by researchers over the past decades, many of whom did not specialize in research methodology. In this sense, the cumulative literature reflects a form of collective theorizing, where each publication contributes a small piece to the evolving understanding (or, on the contrary, misunderstanding) of the concept. While such consensus-based development is valuable for mapping conceptual usage, it also highlights the need for more rigorous theoretical and empirical scrutiny, in order to establish more precise operational definitions. Compounding this issue, most works included in this systematic review were not explicitly about the crud factor; rather, many referred to it to dismiss small, yet possibly meaningful effect sizes (e.g., Burke, 1999). The majority of the included works contributed to only a few categories, thus resulting in a sparse matrix of perceived attributes (see the bars for the "no comment" coding category in Figure 5). Additionally, the evolving nature of the literature on the crud factor presents an inherent limitation, as the field continues to develop and accumulate citations. For the sake of specificity, this systematic review included only work explicitly referencing the terms crud factor or ambient noise, excluding studies that implicitly used these concepts or explored related ideas without explicitly labelling them as crud factor.

For example, Gandhi et al. (2024) suggested that the perceived magnitude and importance of a focal relationship may be exaggerated because researchers temporarily neglect the many other variables and moderators that also influence the outcome. Although Gandhi et al. (2024) did not explicitly refer to the crud factor, such networks of interacting and covarying influences are compatible with the idea that observed associations are embedded in complex systems of interconnected variables.

5. Conclusion

Meehl's crud factor and Lykken's ambient noise are, among the works that permitted an inference about their relationship (k = 81), almost uniformly treated as one and the same phenomenon and may therefore be best understood as a case of a jangle fallacy. For the sake of simplicity, we suggest using crud factor as the umbrella term, with ambient noise treated as an interchangeable label in current usage. Both concepts have most frequently been cited to criticize the reliance of NHST on exact-zero effects for testing theories. Building on this synthesis, we propose a new operational definition that integrates the phenomenon into the MTMM framework. Specifically, in its narrow sense, the crud factor refers to correlations between different traits measured by different methods (i.e., heterotrait-heteromethod covariance) that cannot be reasonably explained by substantive theory or by theories of methodological artifacts. In its broad sense, the crud factor additionally includes correlations between different traits measured with the same method (i.e., heterotrait-monomethod covariance), thereby encompassing both the narrow-sense covariance and covariance attributable to method artifacts.

Declaration of AI use.

ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (model claude-opus-5-5; Anthropic) were used to help write the R code for the figures and for data management, based on the first author's own drafts. Claude was additionally used for (i) language editing (grammar and spelling); (ii) formatting the bibliographic references in the inclusion list and the extraction document, which had initially been exported from Google Scholar; and (iii) plausibility and consistency checks across the extraction document, including comparisons with the inclusion list, identification of potential over-or under-deduplication, and verifying whether exactly one citation intention had been coded for each cited key paper (Meehl, 1990b; Lykken, 1968). All code was checked by the first author, every flagged record was re-examined manually, and all decisions and interpretations are the authors' own. Authors' contributions.

Table 3 Coding criteria for the perceived attributes of the crud factor and ambient noise Category Description Appropriateness of NHST against exact-zero effect to corroborate theories Coded 1 if it is stated that, in at least most cases, NHST against exact-zero effects is useful for corroborating theories. Coded 0 if it is stated that NHST is generally not practical or helpful for theory corroboration, or if the absence of absolute zero relationships in the social sciences is mentioned. Left no comment if no statement regarding the appropriateness of NHST is made. Inclusion of common method variance, experimenter bias, and psychological trait and state variables Each of the three aspects-common method variance, experimenter bias, and psychological trait and state variables-was coded separately using the same decision rule. Coded 1 if the respective aspect was included in the conceptualization of the crud factor or ambient noise. Coded 0 if the respective aspect was explicitly excluded from the conceptualization (e.g., by referring to the crud factor or common method variance as separate explanations). Left no comment if the work provided insufficient information to infer either inclusion or exclusion of the respective aspect. Presence among correlational variables Coded 1 if the naming of the construct or the citation context indicated its presence in correlational research. Coded 0 if the construct was explicitly excluded. Left no comment if the construct was not addressed. If the construct was described as omnipresent, coded 1 for correlational research. Presence among variables of randomized experimental variation Coded 1 if the naming of the construct or the citation context indicated its presence in randomized experimental research. Coded 0 if the construct was explicitly excluded. Left no comment if the construct was not addressed. Research field dependency Coded 1 if the magnitude of the crud factor varied across research fields. Coded 0 if it did not. Left no comment if field dependency was not addressed.

Real as replicable

Coded 1 if the crud factor or ambient noise was described as producing real or replicable effects. Coded 0 if its influence was stated not to be real, either because it was held to be non-replicable or because it was attributed to sampling error or chance. Note that under this criterion real refers to replicability rather than to substantive theoretical meaning, so associations arising from methodological artifacts could still qualify as real. Left no comment if the reality of the focal concept was not addressed.

Interchangeable usage of crud factor and ambient noise Coded 1 if equivalence between the two concepts was implied, either through a verbal cue (e.g., "ambient noise, also called crud factor") or by citing Meehl (1990b) in reference to ambient noise or Lykken (1968) in reference to the crud factor, as such citations presuppose that the two labels denote the same phenomenon. Coded 0 if the concepts were clearly distinguished from one another (e.g., "crud factor or ambient noise", where the or marks separate causes); cases of doubt were also coded 0, biasing the coding towards treating the concepts as distinct. Left no comment if only one concept was referred to and no link to the other was implied. Where both concepts were treated synonymously but only one was elaborated upon, the elaboration was attributed to both, resulting in two entries in the extraction file.

Magnitude of the crud factor or ambient noise

A numerical value was recorded where a work reported an estimate of the magnitude of the focal concept, or where the focal concept was invoked to dismiss an effect of a stated size, in which case that effect size was recorded. Where a work gave a range rather than a point value, the upper bound was recorded. Left no comment if no magnitude was stated or implied.
